title: Shavuot: Ruth (Ruth 1:16)
hookLine: Ruth, the Moabite who chose to join: "whither thou goest, I will go"

lines: ONE TURNS BACK. ONE HOLDS ON.
cards: Three widows stand on a road. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem after about ten years abroad, with nothing: her husband and both her sons have died.
The two younger women are her daughters-in-law, both from the land of Moab. Naomi tells them, kindly and firmly: go back to your mothers' houses. You're young.
Marry again. I have nothing left to give you. They weep.
Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye and turns back, and the book doesn't blame her for it. Ruth holds on, and won't let go.

teach.h: ENTREAT ME NOT TO LEAVE THEE.
teach.b: What Ruth says next has been quoted at weddings, conversions and gravesides.

In the old Jewish translation: "Entreat me not to leave thee," she begins, then: "for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Only death, she adds, will part them. Notice the order: a person, then a people, then God. Jewish tradition came to see her as the model of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice.
They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Ruth gleans in the fields of a relative named Boaz, who treats her with care, and in the end they marry. Their son is Obed.
Obed's son is Jesse. And Jesse's son, the book ends, is David, the king.
So the great king of Israel had a great-grandmother from Moab, a foreigner who chose to stay. Why read it on Shavuot? Several reasons are given.

The story runs through the harvest, from barley to wheat, and Shavuot is the wheat harvest festival. Ruth accepts the Torah freely, as Israel did at Sinai. And a tradition holds that David was born and died on Shavuot.
A midrash adds one more: this little book has no laws of purity or impurity; it was written only to teach how great the reward is for those who do kindness.
Chesed, loving-kindness, runs through every chapter: Ruth to Naomi, Boaz to Ruth, and Naomi, who in the end holds the baby close.

how: On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read in the synagogue, in some communities on the second day outside Israel; Ruth is honored as the model of a person who joins the Jewish people by choice.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and your mother-in-law Naomi tells you to go back to Moab and start over. what do you do?
o: go back to your mother's house, like Orpah.
go with Naomi, to her people and her God.
stay in Moab and send Naomi money.
games.why: whither thou goest, I will go. Ruth chose Naomi, then her people, then her God, and became David's great-grandmother.

practice: Think of someone who didn't have to be in your life but chose to be: a friend who stayed through a hard year, an in-law, a stepparent, someone who joined your family or community.
Picture them on the road with you, holding on, and think how you'd let them know they belong: a word, a seat at your table, an invitation.
